title: Military funerals and the roots of funeral bands
summary: Militia and fraternal funerals, complaints about unseemly music, and Black burial societies.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: What about funeral music in those days? Can you infer anything about it? You come across that?

Well, uh, pre-Civil War days I'm talking about. Pre-Civil War days. The, the, uh, the beginning, sort of, with the great love they had for military funerals here and all that. You see, they had all these veterans of the battle of, uh, January 15th, and there were, uh, uh, 1815, January 8th, 1815, the, the battle of New Orleans. And, uh, uh, uh, uh, even before that battle there was a great, uh, militia tradition here. And almost everyone was organized into this, that, or the other militia company, which loved to have a different uniform, get out and parade, and, uh, had its band usually attached to it. And the militia company wasn't much good without, uh, its own band for parade. In addition, the Masons were very, uh, strong here. And, uh, other French, uh, uh, societies, uh, springing out of the French Revolution, were present here. And then with the advent of, uh, Germans and Irish and other groups, Spanish, they tended to form national groups, usually modeled into something either semi-militia, semi-fraternal, or fully fraternal and semi-military, something like this, uh, Masonic. And, uh, so that by the 1820s, uh, most, uh, most anybody would be able to have a military funeral, because somewhere along that line he belonged to a veterans organization or a fraternal organization or something. And there were a great, great many military funerals, some very long and some, uh, short. And I think this, uh, uh, was, uh, taken over by the Negro, who simply modeled himself after these things. Uh, probably more military funerals here in New Orleans than anywhere else. And if they couldn't get ahold of a body, they still didn't stop from having a military funeral. They had one for Napoleon, and, uh, I believe, I remember, that they had one for Lafayette, too. It's just, uh, a thing to do. And sometimes, uh, uh, more than one ban in these things. Now, you find in the, uh, curious note in the, uh, they had a series of yellow fever epidemics in the 1850s, 1857, a very bad one. And you find, uh, here that plenty of people were being, uh, buried, you see. And a lot of them were buried with these military parades. And you find complaints against these parades on two grounds. One was that there were so many of them, and they made so much noise, they were disturbing the people who were critically ill. But the other one, and this is the really significant one to me, is the fact that editors and reporters, uh, and moralists, complained that these bands, when they came back from the grave, played, and they, these are the exact words, unseemly music. Now, whether that just simply meant that they went off into a rousing good march song coming back, uh, or whether it meant that the music was even, uh, uh, possibly just a hint of a, uh, of a jazzed-up march. After all, all you have to do to, uh, any march that's a melodic march is kind of hit the, hit the off-beats a little harder than usual, and you get a, uh, a jazzed-up feeling to it. It doesn't have to be ad lib. It's like a rag very much.

And, uh, whatever it was, it was unseemly music coming back from the graves. And, of course, you can see how many of these things there were when they had to complain that the noise was continually disturbing the, the patients in the hospitals. That never died out either. And I suppose as the Negroes took over, uh, these customs and, uh, it became the thing to do, of course, uh, you know, today, and especially more so twenty or thirty years ago, uh, many Negroes aspired to belong to one or another, uh, burial or fraternal, uh, organizations to ensure a good, solid funeral, which usually meant possibly a band and a parade.
